column1: What is the fundamental architectural role of a load balancer in horizontal scaling?
column2: It acts as a dispatcher that decides which backend server handles each discrete work unit (connection/request), transforming many independent servers into a unified logical service without itself becoming the bottleneck.

column1: What are the three core operational invariants every load balancer must satisfy?
column2: 1) Traffic distribution (avoid hotspots while preserving affinity where needed), 2) High availability via continuous health checking, 3) Graceful failure handling without exposing errors to clients.

column1: Why can TCP connection state alone not detect a 'zombie backend'?
column2: A zombie backend keeps TCP sockets open (no RST sent) while its application layer has silently stopped processing requests, so only active application-layer health probing—not passive connection tracking—can detect it.

column1: What is the core invariant governing distribution algorithm decisions in a load balancer?
column2: Request-to-backend mapping stability under bounded decision latency: each connection must be assigned to a backend within microseconds using only local state, with no consensus or multi-round negotiation available.

column1: Why do sticky sessions transform load balancing from an optimization problem into a constraint satisfaction problem?
column2: Because once a client-backend binding exists (e.g., session state on one server), subsequent requests must route to that same backend, violating the stateless assumption that any backend can serve any request.

column1: Why does the 'stateless ideal' maximize horizontal scalability in load balancer design?
column2: Because when any backend can serve any request interchangeably, distribution reduces to a pure optimization problem (e.g., minimizing max queue depth), free from session-binding constraints.

column1: What is the central invariant describing the nature of health checks?
column2: Health checks are statistical inference over a noisy channel — a single failed probe doesn't confirm true failure (transient issues), and a single success doesn't confirm true health (e.g., DB pool exhaustion), requiring hysteresis.

column1: Why is hysteresis necessary in health check state machines?
column2: To avoid flapping backends in/out of rotation due to transient network drops or CPU spikes; requiring multiple consecutive failures/successes before changing health state smooths out noise in probe results.

column1: What is the fundamental tradeoff in health check frequency design?
column2: Detection latency vs. system overhead: higher-frequency probing detects failures faster but imposes CPU, bandwidth, and backend handler-thread costs that scale with the number of monitored backends.

column1: Why did early hardware load balancers (F5, Citrix, A10) rely on ASICs/NPUs with CAM/TCAM?
column2: General-purpose CPUs of the era couldn't sustain line-rate packet processing at multi-gigabit speeds; CAM/TCAM structures enabled constant-time connection table lookups regardless of table size, achieving sub-microsecond forwarding.

column1: What is the key architectural tradeoff between hardware and software load balancers today?
column2: Software load balancers (HAProxy, NGINX, Envoy) offer deployment flexibility, CI/CD integration, and horizontal scalability, but incur higher per-packet CPU cost compared to dedicated ASIC/NPU hardware appliances.

column1: How does a Layer 4 load balancer differ from a Layer 7 proxy in connection handling?
column2: Layer 4 rewrites packet headers via DNAT/SNAT to forward the same connection to a backend (single connection, kernel-level), while Layer 7 terminates the client connection and opens a separate backend connection after parsing HTTP headers (dual-connection model, higher memory/latency overhead).
